title: Reconstruction, 1865–1877: Freedom, Citizenship and Backlash
summary: Students follow the nation from the end of the Civil War to the Compromise of 1877. They study the competing plans for reunion, the Freedmen's Bureau, the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, the Black Codes, Radical Reconstruction, the Ku Klux Klan and the end of federal enforcement. Short primary-source excerpts, a Socratic seminar on whether Reconstruction failed, and a document-based essay build the skills of historical argument.
brief: Reconstruction for grade 11 US history: eight 50-minute lessons from the end of the Civil War to the Compromise of 1877: Lincoln's and Johnson's plans, the Freedmen's Bureau, the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, Black Codes, Radical Reconstruction, the rise of the Ku Klux Klan and the end of Reconstruction. Use short primary-source excerpts in every lesson, a Socratic seminar on whether Reconstruction failed, and a document-based essay at the end (50%). Seminar 20%, lesson exit tickets 30%.
policies:
This unit includes sources that describe racial violence and use the language of their time. We read them as evidence, we do not repeat slurs aloud, and anyone may step out for a moment without asking.

Exit tickets are collected every lesson and cannot be made up without an excused absence.

The document-based essay is submitted on paper or through the class site by the start of class on the due date; late essays lose 5% a day.

Quote and cite the documents we read in class. Wording copied from anywhere without quotation marks is plagiarism.

keyIdeas: Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan (December 1863) let a Southern state form a new government once 10% of its 1860 voters swore loyalty to the Union and accepted the end of slavery.
The Wade-Davis Bill (1864) asked for far more: a majority of white men, an ironclad oath, and a state constitution that abolished slavery. Lincoln killed it with a pocket veto on July 4, 1864.
The two plans disagreed over who controls Reconstruction, the president or Congress. Neither plan gave Black men the vote.
Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865) names slavery as the cause of the war, treats the war as a judgment on the whole nation, and asks for peace without malice.

A harsher 1864 plan from Congress. It required a majority of white men to swear loyalty and states to abolish slavery. Lincoln pocket vetoed it.

study.overview: Before the Civil War ended, Americans were already fighting over how the Southern states should return to the Union. Abraham Lincoln offered an easy path in 1863. Congress answered in 1864 with a much tougher bill, and Lincoln blocked it. In March 1865 Lincoln gave his Second Inaugural Address, which explained what he thought the war meant and how the nation should treat the South. This guide covers the two plans, the conflict between them, and the speech.

points.heading: Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan (December 1863)
points.explanation: On December 8, 1863, Lincoln issued a Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction. Union armies held parts of Louisiana, Arkansas and Tennessee, and he wanted an easy way back to shorten the war. A Southerner could swear loyalty to the Union and accept the end of slavery. In return he received a pardon, and his property was restored except for enslaved people. Some high Confederate officers were excluded from pardon. Once 10% of the number of voters in the state in 1860 had taken the oath, the state could set up a new government. The threshold counts 1860 voters, not the whole population. Example (hypothetical): suppose a state had 80,000 voters in 1860. Only 8,000 of them would need to take the oath, even if the state held far more people, including women, children and enslaved people. Louisiana, Arkansas and Tennessee formed governments this way, but Congress refused to seat their members.

points.heading: The Wade-Davis Bill (1864)
points.explanation: Senator Benjamin Wade and Representative Henry Winter Davis were Radical Republicans who wanted tougher terms and a bigger role for Congress. Their bill asked for much more than Lincoln did. A majority of the state’s enrolled white men had to swear to support the Constitution, and only men who could swear the ironclad oath, that they had never voluntarily aided the Confederacy, could vote for or serve as convention delegates. The new state constitution had to abolish slavery. A provisional governor, named by the president, would run the state under rules set by Congress. Example (hypothetical): suppose a state had 90,000 white men. More than 45,000 of them would have to swear to support the Constitution. Under Lincoln’s plan, a small group of loyal men could restart a government, but under this bill a state would have to wait until a majority could swear. Lincoln did not sign the bill. He let it die with a pocket veto on July 4, 1864. That means the president lets a bill expire without signing it when Congress is about to adjourn. Wade and Davis answered with a published protest in August 1864.

points.heading: Who controls Reconstruction, and who was left out
points.explanation: Both plans ended slavery in the rebuilt states, but they disagreed about power. Lincoln’s plan put the president and loyal Southerners in charge. The Wade-Davis Bill put Congress in charge of the rules. So the fight was not only about how strict to be. It was about whether the president or Congress would direct the return of the South. This conflict returns later in the course. The plans also shared a gap. Neither one gave Black men the vote. Example: in a state that followed either plan, a Black man who had just been freed would not have been counted among the voters whose oaths decided whether the state could return.

points.heading: Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865)
points.explanation: Lincoln spoke about five weeks before Lee’s surrender. He did not lay out plans for readmitting states. He explained what the war meant. He named slavery as the cause of the war. He described the war as a judgment on the whole nation, not on the South alone, so North and South shared responsibility. He then asked Americans to finish the war without hatred and to treat the defeated with charity. His best-known line is the opening of the closing paragraph: “With malice toward none.” Example: when you read the speech, find a phrase where Lincoln talks about slavery and the war. Then find a phrase where he talks about how to treat the South once the fighting stops. Each phrase gives you evidence for a different idea in the speech. Notice that the speech says nothing about voting or about terms for readmission, and use that when you compare it with the two plans.

handouts.key:
Corrected first sentence: Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan (December 1863) allowed a former Confederate state to form a new government when people numbering at least 10% of its votes cast in the 1860 presidential election took an oath of loyalty that included support for emancipation.

Corrected second sentence: The Wade-Davis Bill (1864) required a majority of enrolled white male citizens to swear loyalty before reconstruction could proceed, so it imposed stricter terms than Lincoln’s plan. It also required those participating in the constitutional convention process to swear that they had not voluntarily supported the Confederacy.

Why the reversal matters: Reversing the requirements hides Congress’s demand for stricter conditions and its conflict with Lincoln over who would control Reconstruction.

Look for both sentences corrected and an explanation connecting the different requirements to presidential and congressional authority. Common slips: using 10% of the population instead of the 1860 presidential vote; assigning the stricter plan to Lincoln; changing the accurate statement about Lincoln’s pocket veto.

handouts.key:
Slavery and the cause of the war: Lincoln identifies slavery as the cause of the conflict and presents the war’s suffering as possible divine judgment on the nation for slavery. Students should point to his discussion of slavery as the powerful interest behind the war in the paragraph beginning “One-eighth of the whole population,” or his comparison of suffering under slavery with suffering in war in the paragraph beginning “Fondly do we hope”. Look for a clear connection between slavery and the war. Common slip: saying Lincoln treats both sides’ political aims as identical because he describes shared national responsibility.

How the nation should treat the South: Lincoln urges reconciliation without hatred, care for people harmed by the war, and a just, lasting peace. Students should point to “With malice toward none” or paraphrase his call to heal the nation and care for veterans, widows, and orphans in that paragraph. Look for reconciliation linked to justice or care. Common slip: treating this appeal as a detailed readmission plan or a promise of voting rights for Black men.

segments.description:
Explain for about three minutes that Johnson issued his Amnesty Proclamation on May 29, 1865. An oath of loyalty brought a pardon and the return of property, except enslaved people. Fourteen excepted classes, including those with taxable property over $20,000, had to apply to him personally.

study.overview: Andrew Johnson became president on April 15, 1865, the morning Lincoln died, while Congress was not in session. He used that gap to set the terms for bringing the defeated South back into the Union. His choices gave white Southerners control of rebuilding, left freed people without a vote, and reversed the promise of land that General Sherman had made earlier that year. During the same months, the Freedmen’s Bureau began work in schools, labor contracts and relief, with few agents and little money. This guide reviews the plan, the land and the Bureau so you can weigh each one against evidence.

points.heading: Johnson’s pardons and provisional governments
points.explanation:
On May 29, 1865, Johnson issued his Amnesty Proclamation. Most white Southerners could take an oath of loyalty and receive a pardon and their property back. Enslaved people were the exception: they could not be returned to slavery as property. Fourteen excepted classes, including wealthy Confederates with taxable property over $20,000 and high Confederate officials, had to apply for pardon one by one.

Johnson then named provisional governors to rebuild state governments. The steps ran in this order: the governor is appointed; pardoned white men who took the oath elect convention delegates; the convention voids secession, abolishes slavery and repudiates the Confederate war debt; voters then elect a legislature, a governor and members of Congress. New governments also had to ratify the 13th Amendment.

Example (hypothetical, for illustration): suppose a farmer in Alabama owned a modest farm worth well under $20,000 and had fought for the Confederacy. He could take the oath, receive a pardon and vote for convention delegates. His Black neighbor, newly freed and just as much a resident of the state, could not vote at all. Only pardoned white men chose the delegates. When you evaluate Johnson’s plan, look at what it demanded of states and also at who was allowed to decide.

points.heading: Field Order No. 15 and the land that was returned
points.explanation:
On January 16, 1865, General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Orders, No. 15, four days after meeting Black ministers in Savannah, Georgia. The order set aside coastal land for freed families, in plots of up to 40 acres. By mid-1865, tens of thousands of freed people had settled on this land.

The promise did not last. Johnson’s pardons restored property to pardoned owners, and most of the land went back to them. In October 1865, General Oliver O. Howard, head of the Freedmen’s Bureau, traveled to Edisto Island, South Carolina, and told freed people there that the land would be returned.

Timeline to remember: January 16, 1865, Sherman sets aside land. March 3, 1865, Congress lets the Freedmen’s Bureau rent abandoned land in tracts of up to 40 acres. May 29, 1865, Johnson’s pardons begin restoring property. October 1865, freed people on Edisto Island are told to give up the land. Notice what this sequence shows: a pardon was not only a legal act. It also decided who held the land and who did not.

points.heading: What the Freedmen’s Bureau did and what held it back
points.explanation:
Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands on March 3, 1865. It operated under General Howard in the War Department. A small staff of army officers and agents covered the whole South. Its work fell into three areas, and each came with limits.

Schools: Many Black communities started schools on their own. Bureau agents helped find buildings, shared some costs and worked with Northern aid societies that sent teachers south. The Bureau also helped found colleges: Fisk (1866), Howard (1867) and Hampton (1868). Limits: Congress gave little money for education, and in some places white mobs burned schools and threatened teachers.

Labor contracts: Agents supervised written contracts between planters and freed workers and could hear complaints about unpaid wages. Limits: the Bureau urged freed people to sign and return to plantations, many had no land and little choice about terms, and some agents sided with planters.

Relief: The Bureau handed out rations and clothing, ran hospitals and sent doctors where disease spread. Limits: relief was meant to be temporary and was cut back within a few years.

To use this evidence well, pair each action with its limit. Fisk and Howard are examples of an effect that outlasted the Bureau itself, while rations were short-lived. When you judge the Bureau’s overall impact, name a specific detail, say what it shows, and say what it leaves out.

handouts.title: The Freedmen's Bureau at work

blocks.text: Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands on March 3, 1865. General Oliver O. Howard led it from the War Department. Below are three short summaries of its work. Read them as evidence. Two of them mention threats or violence against teachers and Bureau agents. Anyone may step out for a moment without asking.
Schools

Freed people wanted schools, and many Black communities began them on their own. Bureau agents helped by finding buildings, sharing some costs and working with Northern aid societies that sent teachers south. The Bureau also helped found colleges: Fisk (1866), Howard (1867) and Hampton (1868). Congress gave the Bureau limited money for education, so schools depended heavily on aid societies and on freed families who paid what they could. In some places white mobs burned schools and threatened teachers.
Labor contracts

Most freed people had no land and needed work. Bureau agents supervised written contracts between planters and freed workers. The contracts set wages or a share of the crop. Agents could hear complaints when an employer refused to pay or cheated a worker. But the Bureau also urged freed people to sign contracts and return to work on plantations. With no land of their own, many had little choice about the terms. There were few agents for a very large region, and some sided with planters.
Relief

After the war many people in the South were hungry, homeless or sick. The Bureau handed out food rations and clothing to freed people and to some poor white refugees. It also ran hospitals and sent doctors to places where disease spread. Relief was meant to be temporary, and the Bureau cut it back within a few years. Agents who reported abuses sometimes faced threats.
Your notes
After reading, fill in the table. For each area, write what the Bureau did and what limited it. Use the summaries above.
Underline the area in the table that you judge the most lasting. Then write one sentence explaining why.

blocks.hint: Name the area you underlined and give your reason.

handouts.key:
Schools — What the Bureau did: Found buildings, shared some costs and worked with Northern aid societies that supplied teachers. Helped found Fisk, Howard and Hampton. What limited it: Limited federal funding made schools depend on aid societies and freed families’ payments. White mobs burned schools and threatened teachers. Common slip: Saying the Bureau created all schools; many Black communities started schools themselves.

Labor contracts — What the Bureau did: Supervised written contracts setting wages or crop shares. Heard complaints about unpaid wages and cheating. What limited it: Pressured freed people to return to plantation work. Landlessness weakened workers’ bargaining power. Too few agents served a large region, and some favored planters. Common slip: Assuming written contracts guaranteed fair treatment or gave workers land.

Relief — What the Bureau did: Distributed food rations and clothing to freed people and some poor white refugees. Ran hospitals and sent doctors to areas affected by disease. What limited it: Relief was temporary and was reduced within a few years. Agents reporting abuses sometimes faced threats. Common slip: Saying relief served only freed people or provided permanent support.

Most lasting area and explanation — A strong answer underlines Schools and explains that education and institutions such as Fisk, Howard and Hampton could continue benefiting people after temporary relief ended. Accept Labor contracts if the student explains the lasting importance of written employment terms and a way to raise complaints while recognizing weak enforcement. Accept Relief if the student explains that food and medical care could save lives and support recovery despite their temporary availability. The named area must match the underlined row, and the reason must connect a specific action to a lasting effect. Common slip: Naming an area without explaining why its effects could last.

segments.title: The 1865 Black Codes in Mississippi and South Carolina
segments.description:

Texts use period terms; say “freed people” aloud. Students may step out. They read as evidence and never play the people involved.

segments.title: Sort the restrictions: labor, movement, property
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Sort the restrictions: labor, movement, property”.
The sheet has the blank table. Students fill in, alone, one restriction from each state in each row, for four minutes.
In a cell, they write only a rule the text states directly. If a state’s excerpt holds no direct rule for that row, they write “none appears”.
Partners check each other’s cells and fix any that do not match the text, for two minutes.
Hear from two students on the property row.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expected answers, one per line; check against your copies:
Labor, Mississippi: written evidence of a lawful home or employment each January; leaving contracted employment early without good cause meant forfeiting earned wages and possible arrest and return to the employer.
Labor, South Carolina: no trade except farmer or servant without a license fee.
Movement, Mississippi: the vagrancy act let officials arrest idle freed people and fine them.
Movement, South Carolina: servants could not leave the employer’s premises without permission.
Property, Mississippi: personal property allowed, but renting or leasing land or homes permitted only in incorporated towns or cities.
Property, South Carolina: none appears in the servants and trades sections. The license fee limited ways to earn money, which could make buying land harder, but that is an inferred effect, not a rule on holding property. Accept “none appears” for this cell.

segments.title: Work the case backward
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Work the case backward”.
The sheet has the hypothetical case. Explain that students start from the outcome and work back to its cause.
Alone, students write the chain of steps in order, from the first law to the forced labor, in five minutes. They name the law or clause used at each step.
Pairs compare chains and settle one disagreement, for three minutes.
Hear from two pairs, for two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected chain: Samuel, a Black adult over eighteen, had no lawful employment or business on or after the second Monday in January 1866; arrest and conviction for vagrancy; a fine remains unpaid for five days; the sheriff hires him out to someone who pays the fine and costs in return for the shortest period of service. The exception clause permitted compulsory labor as punishment after conviction; the state law supplied the hiring-out mechanism. Leaving contracted employment without good cause followed a different route: arrest and return to the employer. Misconception: that the codes used the word slavery. These provisions used contracts, criminal penalties and hiring-out rather than declaring people enslaved, but they explicitly targeted freed people and other Black residents by race. Convict leasing grew later from this logic.

keyIdeas: The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude across the United States. It made one exception: punishment for a crime of which a person has been duly convicted.

The Black Codes passed in Mississippi and South Carolina in late 1865 let freed people marry, sue and own some personal property. They also restricted where and how freed people could work, where they could go, and what land they could hold.
Vagrancy, contract and license laws turned ordinary acts into crimes. Fines that could not be paid led to people being hired out, which the exception clause allowed. Convict leasing grew from this.
The Black Codes were written by governments that Johnson’s plan left in white hands, with no Black vote. Northern anger at them shaped what Congress did next.

bullets: Prompt: As you read, mark every rule that limits a freed person’s work, travel or land.
slides.notes: Explain for about three minutes that Southern legislatures elected under Johnson’s plan passed new laws in the fall of 1865. These governments were left in white hands, with no Black vote. Say that the laws gave freed people some rights, such as marrying, suing and owning some personal property, but tied them to plantation work and limited the land they could hold. Hand out the excerpts: Mississippi, “An Act to Confer Civil Rights on Freedmen” (Nov. 1865), the sections on labor contracts and on renting land; Mississippi’s vagrancy act (Nov. 1865); South Carolina, “An Act to Establish and Regulate the Domestic Relations of Persons of Color” (Dec. 1865), the sections on servants and trades. Students read for four minutes and mark. Then partners tell each other their two strongest marks, for two minutes. The texts use period terms: say “freed people” aloud. Students may step out. They read as evidence and never play the people involved.

slides.title: Sort the restrictions: labor, movement, property
bullets: Write only a rule the text states directly.
No direct rule for that row? Write none appears.
slides.notes: Hand out the sheet “Sort the restrictions: labor, movement, property”. Students work alone for four minutes, one restriction from each state in each row. Partners then check each other’s cells against the text and fix any that do not match, for two minutes. Hear from two students on the property row. Expected answers, to check against your copies. Labor, Mississippi: written evidence of a lawful home or employment each January; leaving contracted employment early without good cause meant forfeiting earned wages and possible arrest and return to the employer. Labor, South Carolina: no trade except farmer or servant without a license fee. Movement, Mississippi: the vagrancy act let officials arrest idle freed people and fine them. Movement, South Carolina: servants could not leave the employer’s premises without permission. Property, Mississippi: personal property allowed, but renting or leasing land or homes permitted only in incorporated towns or cities. Property, South Carolina: none appears in the servants and trades sections. The license fee limited ways to earn money, which could make buying land harder, but that is an inferred effect, not a rule on holding property. Accept “none appears” for this cell.

slides.title: Work the case backward
bullets: Start from the outcome. Work back to its cause.
Write the chain of steps, first law to forced labor.
Name the law or clause at each step.
Compare chains with a partner. Settle one disagreement.
slides.notes: Hand out the sheet “Work the case backward”. Explain that the case is made up for practice and is not a record of a real person. Students start from the outcome and work back to its cause. Alone, they write the chain of steps in order, naming the law or clause at each step, for five minutes. Pairs compare chains and settle one disagreement for three minutes. Hear from two pairs for two minutes. Expected chain: Samuel, a Black adult over eighteen, had no lawful employment or business on or after the second Monday in January 1866; arrest and conviction for vagrancy; a fine remains unpaid for five days; the sheriff hires him out to someone who pays the fine and costs in return for the shortest period of service. The exception clause permitted compulsory labor as punishment after conviction; the state law supplied the hiring-out mechanism. Leaving contracted employment without good cause followed a different route: arrest and return to the employer. Watch for the misconception that the codes used the word slavery. These provisions used contracts, criminal penalties and hiring-out rather than declaring people enslaved, but they explicitly targeted freed people and other Black residents by race. Convict leasing grew later from this logic.

study.overview: The 13th Amendment was ratified on December 6, 1865. It ended slavery and involuntary servitude across the United States, but it made one exception: punishment for a crime of which a person has been duly convicted. That same fall, legislatures in Mississippi and South Carolina, elected under Johnson’s plan, passed laws now called the Black Codes. These laws gave freed people a few rights but limited their work, travel and land. This guide shows how the exception and the codes fit together, so you can use specific details when you explain what changed in 1865 and what did not.

points.heading: The amendment’s one exception
points.explanation: The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 covered only areas in rebellion, and some places were exempted, including Tennessee. The 13th Amendment went further and ended slavery everywhere in the country. Congress passed it in January 1865, and three-fourths of the 36 states, which meant 27, had to ratify it. The new Southern governments created under Johnson’s plan counted toward that total. The amendment did not ban all forced labor. It allowed involuntary servitude as punishment for a crime after a person was duly convicted. That means the courts, and the state laws that define crimes, decide who can be made to work. For example, suppose a state made it a crime to be without a job and set a fine as the penalty. A person convicted under that law would be a convicted person, and the exception would apply. The exception sets the limit, and state law fills in who falls under it.

points.heading: What the Black Codes allowed and what they restricted
points.explanation: The Black Codes were written by white-controlled legislatures. Black men could not vote, so freed people had no say in the laws. The codes did give some rights, such as marrying and suing in court. They also tied freed people to certain kinds of work and limited where they could go and what land they could hold. In Mississippi, the vagrancy act let officials arrest freed people who were idle and fine them. Mississippi also allowed freed people to rent or lease land or homes only in incorporated towns or cities, which kept them away from farmland. South Carolina’s law on servants and trades barred freed people from any trade except farmer or servant unless they paid a license fee. Suppose a freedman in Charleston wanted to open a small shop. This is a hypothetical example, not a real person. The license rule would stand in his way.

points.heading: How ordinary acts became crimes
points.explanation: The codes did not use the word slavery. They worked through contracts, licenses, vagrancy rules and fines. Each of these turned ordinary acts into offenses: lacking work, working a trade without paying a fee, or leaving a job. Many freed people had little cash, so an unpaid fine could lead to being hired out to an employer who paid it. The hiring-out step is where the exception clause mattered. A conviction made the forced labor legal under the amendment, and state law supplied the method. The laws also named freed people and other Black residents directly, so they were aimed at a race, not at crime in general. Later in the course you will see that convict leasing grew from this same logic.

points.heading: Why the codes mattered beyond the South
points.explanation: Many Northerners saw the codes as an attempt to rebuild slavery under new names. Their anger grew because the laws came from governments that Johnson’s plan had left in white hands. The Union had just won the war, and Northerners did not want the results undone by Southern legislatures. This reaction shaped what Congress did next. When you work with the excerpts, read them as evidence. Ask who wrote each rule, who it targeted, and what a freed person could actually do under it.

blocks.text: Sort the restrictions: labor, movement, property

Use the excerpts from the 1865 Mississippi and South Carolina Black Codes. In each row, write one restriction from each state. Write only a rule the text states directly. If a state's excerpt holds no direct rule for that row, write none appears in the cell.

handouts.key:
Labor — Mississippi: Leaving contracted employment before the contract expired, without good cause, meant losing earned wages. Officials could arrest the worker and return the worker to the employer.
Labor — South Carolina: Black workers needed a license to practice trades or businesses other than farming or contracted service. The annual fee was $10 for mechanics, artisans and other trades, or $100 for shopkeepers and peddlers.
Movement — Mississippi: The vagrancy law exposed Black adults without lawful employment or business to arrest and conviction beginning on the second Monday in January 1866. Accept this as a restriction enforced through detention, rather than a general ban on travel.
Movement — South Carolina: Servants could not leave their employer’s premises without permission.
Property — Mississippi: Freed people could own personal property, but could rent or lease land or homes only in incorporated towns or cities. A statement about permission to own personal property alone does not identify the restriction.
Property — South Carolina: None appears. The servants and trades provisions do not directly restrict property ownership. A licensing fee might reduce money available to purchase land, but that is an inferred effect.
Look for a distinct, directly stated rule in each applicable cell. Common slips include treating Mississippi’s rental restriction as a ban on owning all property and putting an inferred economic effect in South Carolina’s property cell. Sources: [Mississippi Black Codes, civil rights act, §§ 1, 6–7; vagrancy act, § 2](https://teachinglegalhistory.unl.edu/s/oer/item/2089); [South Carolina Black Code, servants and licensing provisions](https://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/exhibits/show/after_slavery_educator/unit_three_documents/document_eight).

handouts.title: Work the case backward

blocks.text: Work the case backward
Suppose the following case. It is made up to help us practice; it is not a record of a real person.

In February 1866, in Mississippi, a freedman over eighteen whom we will call Samuel is working for a planter under a sheriff's order. The planter has paid money to the court on Samuel's behalf, and Samuel may not leave. He receives no wages. Before the employment provision began applying in January 1866, Samuel had been free for months.
Start from this outcome and work back to its cause. Write the chain of steps in order, from the first law to the forced labor. At each step, name the law or clause that was used.

blocks.hint: Write your chain of steps here, in order. Name the law or clause at each step.

blocks.text: Compare your chain with your partner's. Choose one place where you disagreed.

blocks.hint: In one or two sentences, write what you disagreed about and how you settled it.

handouts.key:
Chain of steps:
1. Mississippi’s 1865 vagrancy act classified Black people over eighteen without lawful employment or business as vagrants beginning on the second Monday in January 1866.
2. Samuel lacked lawful employment or business after that date. Officials arrested him, and a court convicted him of vagrancy under that provision.
3. The court imposed a fine. Samuel did not pay it within five days after its imposition.
4. Under the vagrancy act’s hiring-out provision, the sheriff hired Samuel to the person who would pay the fine and costs in exchange for the shortest period of service. In this hypothetical case, that person was the planter.
5. Samuel had to work for the planter for that period. His labor discharged the obligation created by the fine and costs rather than providing wages to him. The 13th Amendment’s exception permitted compulsory labor as punishment following conviction; Mississippi’s law supplied the hiring-out mechanism.
Look for the employment provision, conviction, unpaid fine, five-day interval and sheriff’s hiring-out decision in causal order. The amendment permitted the punishment exception; it did not itself order Samuel’s arrest or hire him out. Common slips include skipping conviction, treating unemployment alone as an automatic labor sentence, or substituting the separate arrest-and-return rule for workers who left a labor contract. Source: [Mississippi Black Codes, vagrancy act, §§ 2, 5](https://teachinglegalhistory.unl.edu/s/oer/item/2089).
Partner disagreement response: Answers vary. Look for a specific disagreement and a resolution grounded in the provisions. For example: We disagreed about whether the sheriff could hire Samuel out immediately after arrest. We resolved it by placing conviction and five days of nonpayment before the hiring-out step.

keyIdeas: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 was Congress’s first answer to the Black Codes. It declared people born in the United States citizens, except Indians not taxed, and gave them equal rights to make contracts, sue and own property.

President Johnson vetoed the Act on March 27, 1866. He said it reached into the powers of the states, that Southern states had no voice in Congress, and that it favored Black people over white people. Congress overrode the veto in April 1866, the first time it passed a major law over a presidential veto.
Republicans worried that a later Congress could repeal an ordinary law. They wrote the 14th Amendment, which passed Congress in June 1866 and was ratified on July 9, 1868.

Section 1 of the 14th Amendment establishes citizenship for people born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction. It also bars states from abridging citizens’ privileges or immunities, depriving any person of life, liberty or property without due process, or denying any person equal protection of the laws. The amendment did not give Black men the vote.

A distinct part of a law or constitution that states one rule or protection.

The rule that a government may not take a person’s life, liberty or property without fair legal procedures.
The rule that a state must apply its laws equally to every person within its borders.

study.overview: In early 1866, Congress tried to answer the Black Codes with a national law, the Civil Rights Act of 1866. President Andrew Johnson vetoed it, and Congress passed it over his veto. Congress then wrote the ideas of the Act into the Constitution as Section 1 of the 14th Amendment. This guide reviews the Act, the three main protections in Section 1, and what the amendment did not do.

points.heading: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the veto
points.explanation: The Act was Congress’s first answer to the Black Codes. It declared people born in the United States to be citizens, except Indians not taxed. It also gave them equal rights to make contracts, sue and own property. Johnson vetoed it on March 27, 1866. A veto can be overridden if two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote for the bill again. Congress did this in April 1866 (Senate April 6, House April 9). It was the first time Congress passed a major law over a presidential veto. Example: suppose a Southern state’s code said a freedman could not sue anyone in court. The Act’s guarantee of an equal right to sue was written to stop exactly that kind of rule. To review Johnson’s three objections, look at the sentences you underlined in his veto message. Then ask yourself why Republicans did not stop once the Act had become law.

points.heading: The Citizenship Clause
points.explanation: Section 1 of the 14th Amendment opens with the words “All persons born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they reside.” Citizenship therefore comes from birth or naturalization on U.S. soil, not from a person’s race. The clause also overturned the Supreme Court’s decision in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857). Example: suppose a baby is born in Georgia in 1870 to parents who were freed five years earlier. Under this clause the child is a citizen of the United States and of Georgia, and no state law can say otherwise.

points.heading: Due process and equal protection
points.explanation: These two clauses limit what a state may do. Due process means a state may not take life, liberty or property without fair legal procedures. Example: suppose a state wanted to jail a man for a crime. It would have to tell him the charge and give him a fair trial first. Equal protection means a state must give every person within its borders the equal protection of its laws. Example: suppose a state charged Black residents a fee to use a public ferry but let white residents cross free. The fee applies a different rule to people because of their race, and that is what the Equal Protection Clause is about. A quick test: if the problem is an unfair process, think due process. If the problem is that the law treats groups differently, think equal protection.

points.heading: Timeline and limits of the 14th Amendment
points.explanation: Congress passed the 14th Amendment in June 1866, two months after the override. It was ratified on July 9, 1868. Johnson urged Southern states to reject it, and Tennessee ratified it. Most other Southern states rejected it, which sets up what happens next time. The amendment did not give Black men the vote. The Equal Protection Clause protects people under the laws of a state. It is not a guarantee of voting rights. Voting comes next time, with the 15th Amendment. Example: a man could be a citizen under Section 1 and still be turned away at the polls in a state that limited voting to white men.

blocks.text: These cases are hypothetical, not real events. Alone, name the clause of Section 1 of the 14th Amendment that each case turns on, and give a reason. Then compare answers with your partner and settle one disagreement.
Case 1
A man born in Ohio is told he is not a citizen.

blocks.hint: Name the clause, then give your reason.

blocks.text: Case 2
A farm is taken from its owner with no notice and no hearing.

blocks.hint: Name the clause, then give your reason.

blocks.text: Case 3
White workers may sign contracts. Black workers may not.

blocks.hint: Name the clause, then give your reason.

blocks.text: Case 4
A town fines only Black residents for vagrancy.

blocks.hint: Name the clause, then give your reason.

handouts.key:
1. Citizenship Clause. A person born in Ohio and subject to U.S. jurisdiction is a citizen of the United States and of the state where that person resides. Look for birth in the United States as the connection. Common slip: Naming equal protection merely because the treatment seems unfair.
2. Due Process Clause. A state or local government cannot deprive someone of property without due process of law. Notice and an opportunity for a hearing are central procedural protections. Look for the connection between the farm, property, and the absence of a fair process. Common slip: Saying that government can never take property.
3. Equal Protection Clause. A state law allowing white workers to sign contracts while denying that right to Black workers treats people unequally because of race. Look for the unequal legal treatment of otherwise comparable workers. Common slip: Naming citizenship instead of the protection against discriminatory laws.
4. Equal Protection Clause. A town cannot impose a vagrancy fine only on Black residents while exempting other residents from the same rule. Look for racially unequal enforcement or legal treatment. Common slip: Naming due process solely because the case involves a fine.
For cases 2 and 3, answers should understand the action as state or local government action; Section 1 restricts states.

study.overview: In March 1867 Congress passed the first Reconstruction Act over President Johnson’s veto and put ten Southern states under army command in five districts. Black men then voted and held office in the South, and in 1870 the 15th Amendment made race an illegal ground for denying the vote anywhere in the nation. The amendment also divided the women’s suffrage movement. This guide reviews the steps of the Act, the first Black officeholders, the wording of the amendment and the 1869 split.

points.heading: The Reconstruction Act of 1867 and the five districts
points.explanation: Congress passed the Act on March 2, 1867. Johnson vetoed it, calling military rule in peacetime unconstitutional, and Congress overrode the veto the same day. The ten Southern states covered were grouped into five military districts, each under an army general. District 1 was Virginia. District 2 was North and South Carolina. District 3 was Georgia, Alabama and Florida. District 4 was Mississippi and Arkansas. District 5 was Louisiana and Texas. The generals were Schofield, Sickles, Pope, Ord and Sheridan. Tennessee was not in any district because it had already ratified the 14th Amendment. Example: Texas lay in District 5, so its commander, General Philip Sheridan, supervised voter registration and elections there. Commanders also protected public order and the rights of freed people. They could use military courts and remove civil officials, though civil governments continued under military authority.

points.heading: The path back into the Union
points.explanation: A state had to follow a fixed sequence to be readmitted. Black and white men registered to vote. They elected a convention, and the convention wrote a new constitution. That constitution had to guarantee Black men the vote. The state then ratified the 14th Amendment, and Congress had to approve the result before the state returned. Example: imagine a state in District 4 that held its convention and wrote a constitution with a voting clause for Black men. It still could not rejoin the Union until it ratified the 14th Amendment and Congress accepted its work. Each step had to be finished, and the order mattered.

points.heading: Black officeholders and Hiram Revels
points.explanation: Once Black men could vote and serve in the new governments, they began to hold office across the South. The best-known early example is Hiram Revels. He was born free in North Carolina and became a minister. The Mississippi legislature chose him for the U.S. Senate, and Democrats objected. The Senate seated him on February 25, 1870, making him the first Black U.S. senator. He took a seat once held by Albert G. Brown. Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi followed him in 1875. A print of 1872, Currier & Ives’s The First Colored Senator and Representatives, In the 41st and 42nd Congress of the United States, shows Black members of Congress in formal portraits. Treat it as evidence of how the public pictured Black officeholders at the time.

points.heading: Reading the 15th Amendment and the 1869 split
points.explanation: The 15th Amendment was ratified on February 3, 1870. It bars the United States and any state from denying or abridging the vote because of race, color or previous condition of servitude. To read it well, ask whether a law’s ground is one of those three named grounds. Suppose a state in 1871 passed a law saying no formerly enslaved man could vote. That law would plainly break the amendment. Suppose another state required all voters to be at least 21. That rule names none of the three grounds, so the amendment does not address it. The amendment also does not name sex, and Section 2 of the 14th Amendment had already put the word male into the Constitution. In 1869 this divided the women’s suffrage movement. Frederick Douglass and Lucy Stone backed the amendment as written. They argued the ballot was urgent for Black men facing violence and that women’s suffrage could follow. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony refused to back an amendment that passed over women. They feared it would lose a chance at suffrage for all. The movement split into two associations. Stanton and Anthony led one, and Lucy Stone and Julia Ward Howe led the other. Some leaders on both sides also made racist arguments. When you write about them, paraphrase those arguments as evidence of the period.

handouts.key:
Part 1
Blank: B.

Sample three-sentence response: The 15th Amendment prohibited the United States and the states from denying or restricting a citizen’s vote because of race, color or previous enslavement. It also gave Congress power to enforce that protection through legislation. It did not establish universal suffrage or prohibit every other voting qualification, so Claim B is stronger.

Look for a distinction between protection against specified grounds of discrimination and an unconditional guarantee that every Black man could vote. Common slip: assuming that Section 2 automatically prevented violations. Another is treating the amendment’s silence about literacy tests and poll taxes as permission to use them for racial discrimination.

Part 2
Position table: The National Woman Suffrage Association opposed ratifying the amendment without protection for women’s voting rights. The American Woman Suffrage Association supported ratification while continuing to seek women’s suffrage.

Either position can support a strong answer. Sample supporting ratification: Supporting the amendment secured an essential constitutional protection for Black men. A cost was accepting an amendment that did not prohibit excluding voters because of sex.

Sample opposing ratification without women’s suffrage: Demanding protection for women challenged the exclusion of women from voting rights. A cost was risking delay or defeat of constitutional protection against racial exclusion from voting.

Look for a clear choice and a historically plausible cost. Common slips: saying that all women supported the same position, that the amendment gave women the vote, or that Black women benefited from its voting protection on equal terms with Black men.

keyIdeas: The Ku Klux Klan began in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865-66 as a club of Confederate veterans. Once Black men could vote, it became a secret terror network. It targeted Black voters, Black and white Republican officeholders, teachers and landowners, in order to restore white Democratic control.

Testimony given to the Joint Select Committee that Congress set up in 1871 put victims’ own accounts before the nation. Historians read it as evidence by asking who spoke, to whom and why, and what the speaker could not know.

The Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871 and the Ku Klux Klan Act made attacks on voting and equal rights federal crimes. They brought federal courts, troops and the suspension of habeas corpus against the Klan.

The Acts were partly effective. Federal force broke up the Klan in places such as South Carolina in 1871-72. Light sentences, high costs, falling Northern will and the 1876 Supreme Court decision in United States v. Cruikshank limited them, and violence continued.

study.overview: The Ku Klux Klan operated as a secret network of night riders in disguise, and Congress answered it with new federal laws. This guide covers three skills for studying that struggle: reading a victim’s testimony as evidence, seeing what powers the Enforcement Acts gave the federal government, and judging how well a law worked. Use them whenever you meet a source or a claim about Reconstruction.

points.heading: Reading testimony as evidence
points.explanation: Historians do not treat a testimony as simply true or false. They ask four questions. Who spoke? To whom? Why? What could the speaker not know? In 1871 Congress created the Joint Select Committee to investigate Klan violence in the South, and it heard from victims directly. Abram Colby, a formerly enslaved man who served in the Georgia legislature, described a night attack on his home. He spoke as a victim, to a committee of Congress, in order to put his experience before the nation. He was a firsthand witness, so he knew what happened to him. But he was attacked by men in disguise. A witness in that position might not be able to say who stood behind the masks, or what the riders planned together beforehand. When you cite testimony, name the speaker and the audience, and say what the source can show and what it cannot.

points.heading: What the Enforcement Acts let Washington do
points.explanation: Congress turned to federal power because state officials in some places could not or would not stop night riders. Three laws followed. The Enforcement Act of May 31, 1870, made it a federal crime to use force, threats or bribes to stop citizens from voting, and federal courts heard the cases. The Second Enforcement Act of February 28, 1871, put federal supervisors at elections in large cities. The Ku Klux Klan Act of April 20, 1871, let the president use troops and suspend habeas corpus. Habeas corpus is the right of a person who is held to be brought before a judge and told the reason. Suspending it let authorities in a troubled area arrest and hold suspects without that usual hearing. Congress claimed its authority from the enforcement clauses of the 14th and 15th Amendments. Why was this needed? Georgia shows the problem. In 1868 its legislature expelled its Black members, and Congress had to make the state undo it. Rights written into the Constitution still needed someone to enforce them.

points.heading: Judging how well a law worked
points.explanation: To judge a law, do not ask only whether things got better. Ask three questions. Where did it work? For how long? What was left unchanged? A drop in incidents is evidence, but it does not by itself show that the underlying problem is gone. Here is a plainly hypothetical case. Suppose a town puts extra police on its streets after a run of burglaries, and burglaries fall for a month. A careful writer would say that the patrols reduced burglaries for that month, and would then check whether the drop lasted and whether the nearby towns saw the same change. A careless writer would say that burglary had ended. Use the same habit with the Enforcement Acts. Read evidence from each side, note the place and the year of every fact, and write a claim that is no broader than the evidence you have. A strong judgment names what the evidence shows and also what it leaves open.

segments.description:

segments.title: Why the North grew weary
segments.description:
Explain for four minutes how the Panic of 1873 began when Jay Cooke & Company failed on September 18, 1873, and the stock exchange closed for ten days. Add that the depression lasted until about 1879, and that voters cared more about work and wages.

segments.title: Redeemers and the White League
segments.description:
Explain for three minutes who the Redeemers were: Southern white Democrats who called retaking state governments redemption. Cover their methods: violence by groups such as the White League, intimidation of Black voters, and fraud, with Mississippi in 1875 as the example. Add that President Grant declined to send troops there, and that by 1876 only South Carolina, Louisiana and Florida still had Republican governments.

Partners compare for one minute, and the teacher hears from one pair in one minute.

Warn students it shows violence, and remind them anyone may step out. Read it as evidence only; no acting out. Expected: a Northern artist, Northern readers, arguing that Klan and White League violence share one aim.

segments.title: The disputed election of 1876

Alone, students write how the dispute might be settled and what Southern Democrats might demand in return, in one minute, and the teacher hears from one student.
Explain for two minutes how Congress created a 15-member Electoral Commission that voted 8 to 7 for Hayes on each dispute. Then explain how Southern Democrats accepted the result. In April 1877 Hayes ordered troops in the statehouses of South Carolina and Louisiana back to their barracks, and the Republican governments there fell.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected predictions: a commission or vote in Congress; Southern Democrats might ask for troops out, federal money for Southern projects, a cabinet seat. Hayes did name a Southerner, David Key, Postmaster General. Historians still debate how much was a deal. Hayes was inaugurated March 5, 1877.

keyIdeas: The Panic of 1873 began when the banking firm Jay Cooke & Company failed in September 1873 and set off a depression that lasted until about 1879. Northern voters turned to jobs and money. Scandals, weariness and the Democratic win of the House in 1874 weakened Northern support for enforcing Reconstruction.

Redeemers were Southern white Democrats who retook state governments through violence, intimidation and fraud. Groups such as the White League helped them. By the 1876 election, Republicans still held governments only in South Carolina, Louisiana and Florida.

A strong thesis makes a claim that someone could argue against. It ranks or links causes instead of listing them, and it rests on specific evidence from the sources.

vocabulary.definition: A financial crisis that began in September 1873 when the banking firm Jay Cooke & Company failed. It led to a long depression.
A long period of falling business, high unemployment and hardship. The one that began in 1873 lasted until about 1879.
Southern white Democrats who worked to take back control of state governments from Republicans in the 1870s.
The name Redeemers gave to their return to power in the Southern states. It often came through violence, intimidation and fraud.
A violent group formed in Louisiana in 1874 that attacked Republican officials and Black voters to put white Democrats in power.
A vote cast by an elector from a state. A presidential candidate needs a majority of them to win.
A group of five senators, five representatives and five Supreme Court justices that Congress created in 1877 to decide the disputed electoral votes.
The settlement that made Hayes president and ended federal troop support for Republican governments in the South.
