handouts.key:
The Panic of 1873: Jay Cooke & Company failed on September 18, 1873. The New York Stock Exchange closed for ten days. The ensuing depression brought business failures and unemployment, shifting voters’ attention toward jobs and wages and weakening support for federal enforcement in the South.

The Amnesty Act of 1872: Congress removed the 14th Amendment’s restrictions on holding office from most former Confederates who were subject to them. This helped former Confederate leaders return to politics and reflected growing Northern support for reconciliation. Common slip: saying the act restored voting rights; it chiefly removed disqualifications from holding office.

Scandals, such as the Whiskey Ring of 1875: Whiskey Ring participants evaded federal liquor taxes with help from corrupt officials. Such scandals damaged confidence in Grant’s administration and distracted attention from protecting Black citizens’ rights. Common slip: claiming Grant personally organized the Whiskey Ring.

The 1874 elections: Democrats won control of the House of Representatives for the first time since before the Civil War. Their victory weakened congressional support for continued Republican Reconstruction policies. Common slip: saying Democrats also won the presidency in 1874; it was a congressional election.

Ranking: Accept any ordering that uses each rank from 1 through 4 once and explains the relative importance of the causes. A defensible ranking is Panic of 1873—1; 1874 elections—2; scandals—3; Amnesty Act—4. Look for a distinction between economic pressure, changed political power, damaged public trust, and reconciliation. Students may connect causes: economic distress helped Democrats win congressional seats. Common slip: treating Northern opinion as unanimous or claiming support for Black rights disappeared immediately.

handouts.title: Which thesis is stronger?

blocks.text: Read the practice question and the two theses. This practice question is not the essay question.
Practice question
Why did the federal government stop protecting Black voters in the South in the 1870s?
Thesis A

The federal government stopped protecting Black voters in the South because of the Panic of 1873, scandals in the Grant administration, Democratic gains in Congress, violence by Southern white groups, and the Compromise of 1877.
Thesis B

Federal protection of Black voters ended mainly because the Panic of 1873 turned Northern voters toward jobs and wages; violence by Southern white Democrats and the Compromise of 1877 then finished a retreat that was already under way.

items: Which thesis is stronger, A or B? Write two sentences saying why.

blocks.hint: Name your choice and give your reasons.

handouts.key:
B is stronger. A suitable response is: Thesis B identifies economic distress as the main cause and explains how violence and the Compromise of 1877 completed an existing retreat. Thesis A names relevant causes but does not explain their relative importance or how they worked together.

Look for an explanation of B’s arguable causal relationship, rather than a preference based on length or wording. Common slip: choosing A simply because it names more factors. A stronger thesis still requires supporting evidence; its claim that economic distress mattered most is an interpretation students must defend.

handouts.title: Plan your own thesis

blocks.text: This work prepares for the Document-based essay, worth 50% of the course grade. Use the essay question on the screen.

items: Write a one-sentence thesis that answers the essay question.

blocks.hint: Your thesis, in one sentence.

items: Name one course document and the evidence in it that supports your thesis.

blocks.hint: The document, and the evidence you would use from it.

handouts.key:
Thesis: Accept a single sentence that directly answers the displayed essay question, makes a defensible historical judgment, and establishes a relationship between Reconstruction’s achievements and limitations. Look for a claim that evidence could support or challenge. Common slips: listing topics, repeating the question, or making an absolute judgment without qualification.

Course document and supporting evidence: Accept one accurately identified course document with specific evidence that logically supports the student’s thesis. Possible evidence includes the 14th Amendment’s citizenship, due process, and equal protection provisions; restrictions on freedpeople’s work or movement in the Black Codes studied earlier in the course; or Colby’s testimony describing Klan violence and intimidation. Hayes’s inaugural address can support a claim about his stated commitment to local self-government and constitutional rights. Common slips: naming a document without identifying evidence, treating a promise as proof of its fulfillment, or using evidence that does not support the thesis.

ready: Teacher: a projected copy of Thomas Nast, The Union as It Was: The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery, Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874
Teacher: copies of the passage from Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address (March 5, 1877), on the Southern states and local self-government, about 200 words, checked for period language beforehand

values.text: The essay must be assigned with a deadline, but no actual due date is specified. Choose the date before teaching so students receive a concrete deadline. What date will the document-based essay be due? The course sources give no date, so the teacher must choose it before teaching and tell students at the close.

l_e522104c8d3d.title: Socratic seminar: did Reconstruction fail?
l_e522104c8d3d.summary: Graded Socratic seminar in which students argue whether Reconstruction failed, using primary-source evidence from the whole unit; a graded exit ticket follows.

t_8d607fbbb443.prompt: The war is nearly won. How should the defeated Southern states come back into the Union? Choice A: quickly, with few conditions. Choice B: only after strong proof of loyalty and a clear end to slavery. Choice C: under army rule for several years. Which do you choose, and why?
followUps: What is the biggest risk of the choice you made?
Who would be helped most by your choice, and who would be left most exposed: formerly enslaved people, Union soldiers, or white Southern families?
What would you say to a classmate who chose a different letter?

t_7b33ea910636.prompt: In December 1863, Lincoln said a Southern state could form a new government once 10% of its 1860 voters swore loyalty and accepted the end of slavery. In 1864, Congress passed the Wade-Davis Bill, which asked for a majority of white men and an ironclad oath. Lincoln pocket vetoed it on July 4, 1864. Who should decide the terms for bringing the defeated states back: the president or Congress?
followUps: Which is the greater danger: terms so easy that old leaders keep power, or terms so hard that no state will accept them?
Neither plan gave Black men the vote. Does that change your answer about who should decide?
Lincoln later asked for peace “with malice toward none.” Can a nation show charity and still demand strict conditions? Why or why not?

t_e8d8e33bd5ba.prompt: A student says Lincoln’s plan required one-tenth of a Southern state’s residents to take an oath. Which correction identifies the group used to set the threshold?

choices.text: The state’s white men in 1863
The state’s voters in the 1864 election
The state’s formerly enslaved residents
The state’s voters in the 1860 election

t_e8d8e33bd5ba.explanation: Lincoln’s threshold was based on one-tenth of the state’s 1860 voters. The state’s white men in 1863 confuses Lincoln’s threshold with the Wade-Davis majority requirement. The state’s voters in the 1864 election uses the wrong election year. The state’s formerly enslaved residents were not the group used to set the threshold.

t_1b7c34af6461.prompt: Which oath did the Wade-Davis Bill require of the men who voted for convention delegates?

choices.text: No voluntary aid to the Confederacy
Future loyalty to the Union
Past support for emancipation
A vote in the 1860 election

t_1b7c34af6461.explanation: The bill required an ironclad oath that the person had never voluntarily aided the Confederacy. Future loyalty to the Union was the oath the enrolled majority swore, not the oath required of men voting for delegates. Past support for emancipation confuses the oath with the bill’s requirement to abolish slavery. A vote in the 1860 election confuses the oath with the voter count used in Lincoln’s plan.

t_4369069139cd.prompt: A state constitution under the Wade-Davis Bill had to abolish slavery.

choices.text: True
False

t_4369069139cd.explanation: The bill required a new state constitution that abolished slavery.

t_7299114dbfe1.prompt: A student writes, “The main difference between the plans was that Lincoln required Black men to vote and Congress did not.” Correct the statement and explain one difference between the plans.
t_7299114dbfe1.answer: Neither plan required voting rights for Black men. Lincoln’s plan used a threshold of 10% of a state’s 1860 voters, while the Wade-Davis Bill required a majority of the state’s white men to swear loyalty and let only men who could take the ironclad oath elect the convention.
t_7299114dbfe1.explanation: Neither plan gave Black men the vote. The plans differed in their loyalty requirements and in the roles they gave the president and Congress.

t_eeca77c2573f.prompt: Which interpretation best fits Lincoln’s explanation of the war in his Second Inaugural Address?

choices.text: Tariffs caused the war, and the South alone bore responsibility.
Slavery caused the war, and the North bore no responsibility.
Slavery caused the war, and the nation shared responsibility.
Disputes over voting caused the war, and both sides shared responsibility.

t_eeca77c2573f.explanation: Lincoln identified slavery as the cause of the war and treated the war as a judgment on the nation. Tariffs caused the war, and the South alone bore responsibility replaces Lincoln’s stated cause and narrows responsibility. Slavery caused the war, and the North bore no responsibility overlooks his treatment of national guilt. Disputes over voting caused the war, and both sides shared responsibility identifies the wrong cause.

t_c91e6d9ef363.title: Lesson exit tickets: Lincoln's plan and the Wade-Davis Bill
t_c91e6d9ef363.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences.
steps: Consider the claim: “Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address shows he would have supported the harsh terms of the Wade-Davis Bill.” State whether you agree, disagree, or qualify the claim.
Explain your judgment using at least one specific detail from the Wade-Davis Bill and one from Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address.
t_c91e6d9ef363.answerKey:
1. A strong response disagrees with or qualifies the claim; another judgment can earn credit if supported by accurate evidence and reasoning.
2. A strong response uses a specific detail from each document and explains the connection. For example, the bill set demanding conditions for reconstruction, while Lincoln called for reconciliation without malice. The address does not set reconstruction terms, so it cannot by itself settle what Lincoln would have supported. A common mistake is to treat the address as a detailed endorsement of the bill or as conclusive proof against every strict condition.

t_36c31e2bd5c4.prompt: Was Johnson’s plan lenient or demanding? One reading says it was lenient: most white Southerners could win a pardon and their property back by taking one oath. The other says it was demanding: states had to void secession, abolish slavery and repudiate Confederate war debt. Which reading is better supported by the Amnesty Proclamation and the steps for building new state governments? Give one specific detail.
followUps: Only pardoned white men chose the convention delegates. Does that change which reading you choose?
People with taxable property over $20,000 had to apply to Johnson personally. Does that make the plan more demanding, or does it just give Johnson more power?
Demanding for whom? What did freed people gain from the plan, and what did they not get?

t_24a39b247974.prompt: Which of the Freedmen’s Bureau’s three areas of work had the most lasting effect: schools, labor contracts or relief? Schools: the Bureau helped found Fisk (1866), Howard (1867) and Hampton (1868), but money was limited and mobs burned some schools. Labor contracts: agents supervised written terms, but the Bureau also urged freed people to return to plantations. Relief: rations, clothing and hospitals, but the Bureau cut them back within a few years. Which would you defend, and why?
followUps: What does lasting mean here: lasting for how many years, and for whom?
Relief ended within a few years. Could it still have had effects that lasted longer?
Most freed people had no land. How did that limit what the Bureau’s labor contracts could do?

t_22224e8c46a7.prompt: A former Confederate official was in a class excepted from Johnson’s general amnesty. What did the official have to do to seek a pardon?

choices.text: Take an oath before a state convention
Apply to the Freedmen’s Bureau
Receive approval from a new state legislature
Apply personally to Johnson

t_22224e8c46a7.explanation: People in excepted classes had to apply personally to Johnson. Take an oath before a state convention confuses the general oath with the separate application; apply to the Freedmen’s Bureau assigns pardon power to the wrong agency; receive approval from a new state legislature assigns that power to the state government.

t_492dfb5fd41f.prompt: Under Johnson’s plan, a freed Black man could vote for delegates to his state’s constitutional convention if he took an oath of loyalty.

choices.text: True
False

t_492dfb5fd41f.explanation: The oath did not give Black men the vote in the conventions. Pardoned white men elected the delegates.

t_5d706bbfb1ca.prompt: Which action did Johnson require a state convention to take as it rebuilt its government?

choices.text: Guarantee voting rights to Black men
Repudiate Confederate war debt
Divide plantations among freed families
Pay pensions to Confederate soldiers

t_5d706bbfb1ca.explanation: Johnson required conventions to repudiate Confederate war debt. Guarantee voting rights to Black men was not required; divide plantations among freed families conflicts with the return of much land to former owners; pay pensions to Confederate soldiers was not a condition Johnson set.

t_cfc7c1f5556a.prompt: Which statement best describes the Freedmen’s Bureau’s work on labor contracts?

choices.text: Agents supervised written terms but often pushed freed people toward plantation work.
Agents divided plantation land but often required freed people to pay rent.
Agents guaranteed equal wages but often left contracts unwritten.
Agents ended plantation labor but often restricted access to schools.

t_cfc7c1f5556a.explanation: Bureau agents supervised written labor agreements, but they often steered freed people back to plantations. Agents divided plantation land confuses labor contracts with land policy; agents guaranteed equal wages overstates the Bureau’s power; agents ended plantation labor reverses its role in directing people toward that work.

t_85dcb0456e4d.prompt: A student argues that the Freedmen’s Bureau’s work in education had no lasting value because some schools were burned. Choose whether you agree or disagree. Support your judgment with one detail about its education work and one limit it faced.
t_85dcb0456e4d.answer: I disagree that its education work had no lasting value. The Bureau helped establish schools and supported the founding of institutions such as Fisk. Its work was limited by violence against schools and by short funding, but those limits did not erase its educational achievements.
t_85dcb0456e4d.explanation: A supported judgment weighs an achievement against a limit. The Bureau helped teachers and schools and supported institutions that lasted, while violence and limited funding constrained its reach. A different judgment can earn credit if it uses accurate details and explains the reasoning.

t_c46b7b417cf0.title: Lesson exit tickets: Johnson's plan and the Freedmen's Bureau
t_c46b7b417cf0.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences.
steps: Consider the claim: “Johnson’s plan gave freed people little, but the Freedmen’s Bureau gave them real help.” State whether you agree, disagree, or qualify the claim.
Explain your judgment using at least one specific detail about Johnson’s plan or Field Order No. 15 and one about the Bureau’s schools, labor contracts, or relief.
t_c46b7b417cf0.answerKey:
1. Accept agreement, disagreement, or a qualified judgment supported by the evidence.
2. A strong response may explain that Johnson required states to abolish slavery but excluded Black men from voting, or that pardons led to the return of most land set aside under Field Order No. 15. It may also explain that the Bureau supported schools or provided food and medical care, while limited funding, violence, or pressure to return to plantations restricted its impact. Common errors include claiming that Black men could vote for convention delegates or that the Bureau gave most freed families permanent land.

t_2d35cd69fb0d.prompt: Under the 13th Amendment, which person could legally be required to perform involuntary labor as punishment?

choices.text: A person duly convicted of a crime
A person without a labor contract
A person who lost a civil lawsuit
A person who refused to rent land

t_2d35cd69fb0d.explanation: The amendment made an exception for punishment after a person was duly convicted of a crime. A person without a labor contract was not necessarily convicted; a person who lost a civil lawsuit was not necessarily convicted of a crime; and a person who refused to rent land was not necessarily convicted of a crime.

t_425f38a98ead.prompt: Which rule appeared in South Carolina’s 1865 Black Code?

choices.text: A servant needed permission to marry a freed person.
A servant needed permission to leave an employer’s premises.
A servant could rent land only in an incorporated town.
A servant could work in any trade without a license.

t_425f38a98ead.explanation: South Carolina restricted servants’ movement by requiring permission to leave an employer’s premises. Permission to marry was not the movement rule studied; renting land only in an incorporated town describes a Mississippi restriction; and working in any trade without a license reverses South Carolina’s trade restriction.

t_0fd60730585a.prompt: Under Mississippi’s 1865 Black Code, a freed person could own personal property even though the law restricted where freed people could rent land.

choices.text: True
False

t_0fd60730585a.explanation: Mississippi allowed freed people to own personal property but limited their renting or leasing of land or homes to incorporated towns and cities.

t_0ebc115412bf.prompt: Suppose a student claims that South Carolina’s requirement for a trade license directly banned freed people from owning land. Explain the mistake and identify what the license rule directly restricted.
t_0ebc115412bf.answer: The license rule directly restricted work in trades other than farming or serving. It did not itself state a rule banning land ownership. The fee might make earning money harder, but that is an inferred effect.
t_0ebc115412bf.explanation: The South Carolina trades provision required a license fee for trades other than farming or serving. A possible effect on buying land is different from a direct rule about holding property.

t_39e4f535adeb.prompt: Under Mississippi’s 1865 labor-contract provisions, what could happen if a worker left contracted employment early without good cause?

choices.text: The worker could lose the right to marry and be returned to the employer.
The worker could lose personal property and be hired by a sheriff at once.
The worker could lose voting rights and be assigned a trade by a court.
The worker could lose earned wages and be arrested and returned to the employer.

t_39e4f535adeb.explanation: Mississippi’s labor-contract provisions allowed earned wages to be forfeited and the worker to be arrested and returned. Losing the right to marry was not the specified penalty; losing personal property and immediate hiring by a sheriff confuses this rule with a separate hiring-out process; and losing voting rights and court assignment to a trade were not the specified penalties.

t_a58c7ec02c2b.prompt: In your own words, who could still be forced to work under this amendment, and how would a person become one of them?
followUps: Which words in Section 1 of the 13th Amendment made you say that?
Who decides whether a person has been duly convicted, and what power does that give them?
If a state legislature can decide what counts as a crime, what could happen to the exception over time?

t_d993085af84b.prompt: The 1865 Mississippi and South Carolina laws let freed people marry, sue and own some personal property. They also limited where freed people could work, where they could go and what land they could rent. Were these laws a real step away from slavery, or a new way of controlling Black labor? Use a rule from the excerpts to support your view.
followUps: Which single rule in the excerpts weighs most for your position, and why?
Does a law that grants a right cancel out a law that limits work, travel or land? Who gains and who loses?
These laws were written by governments elected without Black voters. How might that change how we read them?

t_cd78a418c888.title: Lesson exit tickets: The 13th Amendment and the Black Codes
t_cd78a418c888.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences.
steps: Consider the claim: “The 13th Amendment ended forced labor for freed people in the South in 1865.” State whether you agree, disagree, or qualify the claim.
Explain your judgment using one detail about the amendment’s exception clause and one detail about the Black Codes’ limits on labor, movement, or property.
t_cd78a418c888.answerKey:
1. A strong answer disagrees with or qualifies the claim: the amendment abolished slavery and involuntary servitude but allowed involuntary servitude as punishment after a person was duly convicted of a crime.
2. A strong answer connects that exception to an accurate Black Code restriction, such as Mississippi’s vagrancy provisions and the hiring out of a person convicted and unable to pay a fine. The amendment supplied the exception; Mississippi law supplied the hiring-out mechanism. Watch for claims that the amendment banned all forced labor or that every Black Code restriction alone required a conviction. Score each student’s written response after class using both rubric criteria.

t_74a5753c628e.prompt: Congress passes a law and the president vetoes it. Can the law still take effect?
followUps: If a veto were always final, what power would one person hold over the whole Congress?
Why might the Constitution ask for two-thirds of both the House and the Senate to override, and not just a simple majority?
In April 1866, the Senate voted on April 6 and the House on April 9. What does an override on a major law tell you about how strongly Congress felt?

t_370af6e50e6a.prompt: President Johnson argued that the Southern states had no members in Congress, so Congress should not pass the Civil Rights Act of 1866 yet. Was he right that Congress should wait?
followUps: Which sentence in Johnson’s veto message gives the best support for your view, and which sentence works against it?
The Black Codes had already limited freed people’s rights to make contracts and own property. Does that change your answer about waiting?
Who should decide when the Southern states have a full voice in Congress again: the president, Congress or the states themselves? Why?

t_6fc217869033.prompt: What happened after President Johnson vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866?

choices.text: Congress accepted the veto, and the bill failed.
The Supreme Court overrode the veto, and the bill became law.
Congress overrode the veto, and the bill became law.
Southern states overrode the veto, and the bill became law.

t_6fc217869033.explanation: Congress overrode Johnson’s veto in April 1866. “Congress accepted the veto, and the bill failed” reverses the outcome; “The Supreme Court overrode the veto, and the bill became law” assigns Congress’s power to the Court; “Southern states overrode the veto, and the bill became law” assigns that power to the states.

t_a6d863844211.prompt: Which objection did Johnson make when he vetoed the Civil Rights Act?

choices.text: The bill left too much power with the states.
The bill failed to give Black men the vote.
The bill made it harder for Congress to pass laws.
The bill intruded on powers belonging to the states.

t_a6d863844211.explanation: Johnson argued that the bill intruded on state powers. “The bill left too much power with the states” reverses his objection; “The bill failed to give Black men the vote” confuses the Act with a later voting rights issue; “The bill made it harder for Congress to pass laws” does not describe his stated objection.

t_53e0c1f4525c.prompt: Suppose a person is naturalized in the United States and is subject to its jurisdiction. The 14th Amendment says that person cannot be a citizen because they were born elsewhere.

choices.text: True
False

t_53e0c1f4525c.explanation: The Citizenship Clause includes people naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction, as well as people born there and subject to its jurisdiction.

t_b8b7791926f3.prompt: Suppose a state takes a resident’s property without notice or a hearing. Which clause most directly addresses the lack of legal procedures?

choices.text: The Due Process Clause
The Citizenship Clause
The Equal Protection Clause
The Privileges or Immunities Clause

t_b8b7791926f3.explanation: Due process addresses a state’s deprivation of life, liberty or property without fair legal procedures. “The Citizenship Clause” defines citizenship; “The Equal Protection Clause” concerns equal protection of the laws; “The Privileges or Immunities Clause” bars states from abridging citizens’ privileges or immunities.

t_6d75be02cc54.prompt: Suppose a state allows white residents to use its public courts but bars Black residents from using them. A student says, “This is only a citizenship issue because the 14th Amendment says nothing about equal treatment under state laws.” Find the mistake and explain which clause addresses the situation.
t_6d75be02cc54.answer: The mistake is saying that the 14th Amendment says nothing about equal treatment under state laws. The Equal Protection Clause requires a state to give every person within its jurisdiction equal protection of its laws. Barring Black residents from courts while allowing white residents to use them raises an equal protection issue.
t_6d75be02cc54.explanation: The Citizenship Clause defines who is a citizen, but Section 1 also requires states to provide equal protection of the laws to every person within their jurisdiction.

t_9cbf9c273f4c.title: Lesson exit tickets: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment
t_9cbf9c273f4c.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences.
steps: Explain how the Civil Rights Act of 1866 led to the 14th Amendment.
Name one clause from Section 1 of the 14th Amendment and explain what it protects. Give one detail from Johnson’s veto or Congress’s override.
t_9cbf9c273f4c.answerKey:
1. A strong answer explains that Republicans sought constitutional protection for civil rights because a later Congress could repeal the Act and its constitutionality was in doubt.
2. A strong answer accurately explains citizenship, due process or equal protection and gives a correct detail about Johnson’s veto or the congressional override. A common mistake is to say that the 14th Amendment gave Black men the vote.

t_fceb68aeb891.prompt:
By early 1867, ten of the eleven former Confederate states had rejected the 14th Amendment. Only Tennessee had ratified it. What should Congress do?
A. Accept the governments Johnson set up and wait for the Southern states to change their minds.
B. Put the rejecting states under army command until they form new governments on Congress’s terms.
C. Drop the 14th Amendment, because the Southern states refused it.
followUps: If Congress chose A, what would happen to freed people in the South while it waited?
President Johnson vetoed the Reconstruction Act and called military rule in peacetime unconstitutional. Is that a strong reason to reject B?
If Congress chose C, what would that tell Tennessee, the one state that had ratified the amendment?

t_d75b37307ccb.prompt: In 1869, Frederick Douglass and Lucy Stone backed the 15th Amendment as written, saying the ballot was urgent for Black men facing violence and that women’s suffrage could follow. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony refused to back an amendment that passed over women. The 14th Amendment had already put the word male into the Constitution. If you had been in the movement in 1869, which side would you have joined, and what would your choice have cost?
followUps: How much should urgency count when one group is in danger now and another group is asking for a right later?
Supporters said women’s suffrage could follow. What would you want to see before you trusted that promise?
Some leaders on one side used racist arguments to make their case. Does that change how you judge their position, or can the position be judged apart from the arguments?

t_34dffcbca0bb.prompt: Under the Reconstruction Act of March 2, 1867, how were the former Confederate states treated?

choices.text: Eleven states were placed in five military districts, including Tennessee.
Ten states were placed in ten military districts; Tennessee was excluded.
Ten states were placed in five military districts; Tennessee was excluded.
Eleven states were placed in ten military districts, including Tennessee.

t_34dffcbca0bb.explanation: The act placed ten states in five districts. Tennessee was excluded because it had ratified the 14th Amendment. “Eleven states were placed in five military districts, including Tennessee” overlooks Tennessee’s exclusion; “Ten states were placed in ten military districts; Tennessee was excluded” gives each state a district; “Eleven states were placed in ten military districts, including Tennessee” gets both the number of districts and Tennessee’s status wrong.

t_eff52695a22f.prompt: A state held a convention elected by Black and white men, adopted a constitution guaranteeing Black men the vote, and ratified the 14th Amendment. What further step did it need for readmission under the Reconstruction Act?

choices.text: Approval from Tennessee
Ratification of the 15th Amendment
Election of a Black U.S. senator
Approval from Congress

t_eff52695a22f.explanation: Congress had to approve the state’s readmission. “Approval from Tennessee” confuses another state’s ratification with Congress’s authority; “Ratification of the 15th Amendment” substitutes a later amendment for the 14th; “Election of a Black U.S. senator” describes a gain in political representation, not a readmission condition.

t_edf8d83188ff.prompt: After the 15th Amendment was ratified, a state could still set voting rules that did not explicitly deny the vote because of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.

choices.text: True
False

t_edf8d83188ff.explanation: The amendment barred denial or abridgment on those named grounds, but it left states able to set other voting rules.

t_e1c3e6e311b8.prompt: A student claims that ratification of the 15th Amendment settled the question of voting rights for women. Explain why the claim is inaccurate, using the amendment’s scope and the split among suffrage leaders.
t_e1c3e6e311b8.answer: The amendment barred denial of the vote because of race, color, or previous condition of servitude, but it did not name sex. In 1869, some suffrage leaders supported the amendment as written, while others opposed it because it passed over women.
t_e1c3e6e311b8.explanation: The amendment established a national rule against racial denial of voting rights without guaranteeing women the vote. The disagreement over that omission split the women’s suffrage movement.

t_9fda7e3ed0c7.prompt: Which statement best describes a disagreement among women’s suffrage leaders in 1869?

choices.text: Some supported the amendment as written; others opposed it for passing over women.
Some supported military districts; others opposed ratifying the 14th Amendment.
Some supported voting by Black men; others sought to exclude all men from voting.
Some supported congressional readmission; others wanted Tennessee placed under military rule.

t_9fda7e3ed0c7.explanation: Leaders disagreed over whether to support the 15th Amendment without a guarantee of women’s suffrage. “Some supported military districts; others opposed ratifying the 14th Amendment” shifts the issue to Reconstruction policy; “Some supported voting by Black men; others sought to exclude all men from voting” misstates the demand for women’s suffrage; “Some supported congressional readmission; others wanted Tennessee placed under military rule” confuses the suffrage split with state readmission.

t_375e9a9d1b90.title: Lesson exit tickets: Radical Reconstruction and the 15th Amendment
t_375e9a9d1b90.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences.
steps: Explain why Congress created the five military districts under the Reconstruction Act of 1867.
Assess the 15th Amendment: give one gain and one limit, each with a detail.
t_375e9a9d1b90.answerKey:
1. A strong answer explains that Congress sought to replace governments that had rejected the 14th Amendment and to establish new governments under congressional conditions. Military commanders supervised the process and protected public order and freed people’s rights. A common mistake is to say the districts applied to all eleven former Confederate states; Tennessee was excluded.
2. A strong answer identifies the national ban on denying or abridging the vote because of race, color, or previous condition of servitude as a gain. It explains a limit, such as the amendment’s failure to name sex or its leaving other voting rules to states. A common mistake is to claim the amendment eliminated every barrier to voting.

t_e667ac37ff31.prompt: Why would a Black Republican officeholder have been a target of the Ku Klux Klan?

choices.text: The officeholder represented Confederate power the Klan wanted to protect.
The officeholder enforced the Black Codes the Klan wanted to repeal.
The officeholder represented political power the Klan wanted to remove.
The officeholder enforced the Reconstruction Acts the Klan wanted to expand.

t_e667ac37ff31.explanation: The Klan used terror against people who held or supported new political power for Black Americans. “The officeholder represented Confederate power the Klan wanted to protect” confuses Republican officeholders with former Confederate leaders. “The officeholder enforced the Black Codes the Klan wanted to repeal” reverses the Klan’s opposition to Black rights. “The officeholder enforced the Reconstruction Acts the Klan wanted to expand” mistakes the Klan’s hostility to Reconstruction for support.

t_ae227b7a97b5.prompt: A historian can use one victim’s testimony alone to determine how common Klan attacks were across the South.

choices.text: True
False

t_ae227b7a97b5.explanation: A victim’s account can provide firsthand evidence of an attack, but one account alone cannot establish how widespread similar attacks were.

t_1546f50702e1.prompt: Suppose a state government refuses to prosecute a group that has conspired to deny citizens equal protection. Which federal response did the Ku Klux Klan Act allow?

choices.text: Repeal of the 14th Amendment
Automatic removal of the state legislature
A ban on all state elections
Federal prosecution of the conspiracy

t_1546f50702e1.explanation: The Ku Klux Klan Act made conspiracies to deny equal protection a federal crime. “Repeal of the 14th Amendment” reverses the act’s purpose of enforcing rights. “Automatic removal of the state legislature” confuses federal enforcement with replacing a state government. “A ban on all state elections” confuses protecting political rights with suspending elections.

t_60a92387e789.prompt: A historian finds that federal prosecutions reduced Klan activity in one county, while later reports describe political intimidation in a neighboring county. A student writes, “The prosecutions ended political violence everywhere.” Identify the mistake and rewrite the claim in one or two sentences using both pieces of evidence.
t_60a92387e789.answer: The claim treats a local reduction as proof that violence ended everywhere. Federal prosecutions reduced Klan activity in one county, but later intimidation in a neighboring county shows that political violence continued.
t_60a92387e789.explanation: The two observations support a limited conclusion: enforcement could reduce Klan activity in a particular place, while violence could continue elsewhere. They do not establish that violence ended everywhere.

t_6390bf8cab24.prompt: Which group formed the Ku Klux Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee?

choices.text: Confederate veterans
Freedmen’s Bureau agents
Black Union veterans
Federal election supervisors

t_6390bf8cab24.explanation: Confederate veterans formed the Klan as a club in Pulaski in 1865–66. “Freedmen’s Bureau agents” confuses the Klan with a federal agency. “Black Union veterans” confuses the founders with people whose rights the Klan opposed. “Federal election supervisors” confuses the Klan with officials later authorized to oversee some elections.

t_4ff8566f9d35.prompt: The Klan targeted Black voters, Black and white Republican officeholders, teachers and schools, and Black families who owned land or refused unfair labor contracts. Which target was most dangerous to Reconstruction, and why?
followUps: Black men could vote and hold office only because of the new laws and amendments. Why would a campaign of fear against voters and officeholders threaten Reconstruction faster than an attack on one family?
Why might attacking teachers and schools or Black landowners be just as damaging in the long run, even if fewer people noticed it at the time?
The Klan’s aim was to restore white Democratic control. Which target did the Klan most need to silence to reach that aim, and how do you know?

t_2dca874793d2.prompt: In October 1871 President Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties, so that suspected Klan members could be arrested and held. Local sheriffs and juries would not act against the Klan. Was it right for Congress to give the president this power?
followUps: Habeas corpus protects a person from being held without a charge. What could go wrong if a president can set it aside, and who might be harmed?
If state officials will not act and local courts cannot be trusted, what other way could Congress have protected Black citizens and officeholders?
Does it matter that the power was meant for a particular emergency in particular counties? Can a power like this be limited, and how?

t_e3ebfe253055.title: Lesson exit tickets: The Ku Klux Klan and the Enforcement Acts
t_e3ebfe253055.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences.
steps: Explain why the Ku Klux Klan formed and name two groups of people it targeted.
Assess the Enforcement Acts: give one detail that shows they worked and one that shows they fell short.
t_e3ebfe253055.answerKey:
1. A strong answer explains that the Klan sought to restore white Democratic control through fear and names two targets, such as Black voters, Republican officeholders, teachers, or Black landowners. A common mistake is to describe its targets without explaining its political purpose.
2. A strong answer assesses the Acts as partly effective, using a success such as federal arrests in South Carolina in 1871 and a limit such as continued violence at Colfax or the Cruikshank decision. A common mistake is to treat the decline in Klan raids as a permanent end to political violence.

t_1cd646854321.prompt: How did the Panic of 1873 weaken Northern support for enforcing Reconstruction?

choices.text: It persuaded Congress to repeal the 14th Amendment.
It ended violence against Black voters in the South.
It gave Republicans control of the House in 1874.
It shifted voters’ attention toward jobs and wages.

t_1cd646854321.explanation: The depression made economic concerns more urgent for many Northern voters. “It persuaded Congress to repeal the 14th Amendment” is wrong because the amendment remained in force. “It ended violence against Black voters in the South” reverses the pattern of continuing intimidation. “It gave Republicans control of the House in 1874” confuses the result: Democrats won control.

t_f006f10d64ca.prompt: A voter could continue to support Black citizens’ rights while giving greater priority to economic problems during the depression.

choices.text: True
False

t_f006f10d64ca.explanation: Northern support did not disappear all at once. Some voters still supported Black citizens’ rights but placed greater priority on jobs, wages, and other concerns.

t_936910cbf314.prompt: What happened after President Hayes ordered federal troops away from the statehouses in South Carolina and Louisiana?

choices.text: The Republican state governments there fell.
The Electoral Commission reopened the disputed vote.
The federal government repealed the 15th Amendment.
The Freedmen’s Bureau took control of both states.

t_936910cbf314.explanation: The troop withdrawal removed support for the remaining Republican governments in those states, and they fell. “The Electoral Commission reopened the disputed vote” is wrong because the commission had already awarded the disputed votes. “The federal government repealed the 15th Amendment” is wrong because the amendment remained in force. “The Freedmen’s Bureau took control of both states” confuses the bureau’s role with control of state governments.

t_a6afffe83a76.prompt: Which statement best connects the disputed 1876 election to the end of federal troop support for Southern Republican governments?

choices.text: Tilden became president after the commission’s decisions, then withdrew troops from two Southern statehouses.
Hayes became president after the commission’s decisions, then withdrew troops from two Southern statehouses.
Hayes became president after winning the popular vote, then sent troops to two Southern statehouses.
Tilden became president after winning the popular vote, then sent troops to two Southern statehouses.

t_a6afffe83a76.explanation: The commission awarded the disputed electoral votes to Hayes, who later withdrew troops from the South Carolina and Louisiana statehouses. “Tilden became president after the commission’s decisions, then withdrew troops from two Southern statehouses” names the wrong president. “Hayes became president after winning the popular vote, then sent troops to two Southern statehouses” mistakes both the popular-vote result and the action Hayes took. “Tilden became president after winning the popular vote, then sent troops to two Southern statehouses” correctly identifies the popular-vote leader but names the wrong president and action.

t_0543ceb58b61.prompt: A student proposes this thesis for a practice question about why federal support for Reconstruction weakened: “The Panic of 1873, political scandals, and Redeemer violence all mattered.” Explain how the student could make the thesis stronger, then rewrite it as an arguable claim that links or ranks those causes.
t_0543ceb58b61.answer: The thesis lists causes but does not explain their relationship or relative importance. One stronger version is: “The Panic of 1873 weakened federal support for Reconstruction most by shifting Northern voters’ priorities, while scandals and Redeemer violence made continued enforcement harder to sustain.”
t_0543ceb58b61.explanation: A strong thesis makes a claim someone could challenge and explains how causes relate or which mattered most. Other reasoned rankings can work if they can be supported with specific course evidence.

t_cd60919a9cde.title: Document-based essay
t_cd60919a9cde.prompt: To what extent did Reconstruction secure freedom and citizenship for Black Americans? Write an essay of about 500–700 words that weighs gains against limits and losses from 1865 through 1877. This is your own work and counts toward the Document-based essay component, 50% of the course grade. Quote and cite the documents read in class; put quotation marks around any copied wording. The essay is due by the start of class on the due date.
steps: Write an introduction with a thesis that answers the question. Make a claim a reader could dispute and explain how you weigh Reconstruction’s gains against its limits or losses.

Develop your argument in body paragraphs using specific evidence from at least three course documents. You may use the 13th Amendment, the Black Codes, the 14th Amendment, the 15th Amendment, Abram Colby’s testimony, or Hayes’s inaugural address. Explain how each piece of evidence supports or complicates your claim.

Address a different interpretation of Reconstruction and explain why your thesis is more convincing. In a conclusion, connect the gains and losses you have discussed to the end of federal troop support for Southern Republican governments.
t_cd60919a9cde.answerKey:
1. A strong thesis makes a defensible judgment about the extent of Reconstruction’s achievements and weighs constitutional gains against restrictions, violence, or weakened enforcement. There is no single required conclusion. Common mistakes include merely listing events or claiming that all rights disappeared in 1877.
2. A strong essay uses specific evidence from at least three course documents and explains its relevance. For example, it might connect the 13th Amendment’s abolition of slavery and exception clause with Black Code restrictions, then use the 14th Amendment’s citizenship and equal protection provisions or Colby’s testimony to show both gains and threats. Other supported selections are valid. Common mistakes include treating the 14th Amendment as granting Black men the vote, treating testimony as proof of every person’s experience, and quoting without quotation marks or citation.
3. A strong response fairly considers a different interpretation, answers it with evidence, and connects its judgment to Hayes’s 1877 withdrawal of troops from the South Carolina and Louisiana statehouses and the fall of those Republican governments. A strong conclusion distinguishes the loss of troop support from the repeal of constitutional amendments. Common mistakes include treating the inaugural address as proof of later events or claiming that all federal protection and Black political participation ended immediately.

t_794b7caea85d.title: Lesson exit tickets: Redemption and the Compromise of 1877
t_794b7caea85d.prompt: Lesson exit tickets count for 30% of the course grade. Work alone in class. Write four to six sentences. Your work is scored using the rubric below.
steps: Explain how Redeemers regained control of Southern state governments. Give one specific example of a method they used.
Explain how the disputed election of 1876 was settled. Connect that settlement to one cause of the Northern retreat from Reconstruction other than the Panic of 1873.
t_794b7caea85d.answerKey:
1. A strong response explains that Southern white Democrats regained state governments through violence, intimidation and fraud. It may identify the White League or intimidation of Black voters in Mississippi in 1875. Avoid treating their victories as the result of fair elections alone.
2. A strong response explains that a 15-member Electoral Commission awarded the disputed electoral votes to Hayes by 8–7 votes. It connects the settlement to another cause, such as Democratic gains in the 1874 House elections, scandals or weariness with enforcement. A strong connection explains how weakened Northern support made continued federal enforcement less likely. Avoid presenting the details of an explicit bargain as settled fact.

f_704268288233.question: What is a pocket veto, and why did Lincoln use one on the Wade-Davis Bill?
f_704268288233.answer: A pocket veto happens when a president does not sign a bill at the very end of a congressional session. The bill then dies without being sent back to Congress. Lincoln let the Wade-Davis Bill die this way on July 4, 1864. He did not want to cancel the governments already formed under his own plan, and he did not want to commit himself to one fixed set of terms.

f_1030a211c623.question: Why did Lincoln want an easy path back into the Union while the war was still going on?
f_1030a211c623.answer: By late 1863, Union armies held parts of Louisiana, Arkansas and Tennessee. Lincoln hoped that a simple, quick way to form loyal state governments would persuade more Southerners to stop supporting the Confederacy. He thought this could shorten the war.

f_76cdf4480805.question: Why did Congress refuse to seat members from states set up under Lincoln’s plan?
f_76cdf4480805.answer: Many Republicans in Congress believed they, not the president, should set the terms for readmitting Southern states. Each house of Congress decides who may take a seat in it, so Congress could refuse the new members. This is why the fight over the two plans was about who controls Reconstruction as well as how strict the terms should be.

f_626d8bfe7bb2.question: Why didn’t Congress step in while Johnson was setting up the new Southern governments?
f_626d8bfe7bb2.answer: Congress was not meeting when Lincoln died. It was not due to return until December 1865, and Johnson did not call it back early. He used that gap to appoint provisional governors and start the process of rebuilding state governments. By the time members returned, he had already set that process in motion.

f_1e861e97dcca.question: The Bureau handout and the Field Order timeline name General Oliver O. Howard. Who was he, and why does a university carry his name?
f_1e861e97dcca.answer: Howard was a Union general who led the Freedmen’s Bureau from the War Department. The Bureau helped found Howard University in Washington, D.C., in 1867, and the school was named for him. He later served as its president.

f_f0c42edbd803.question: Some sources use an old term for Black people. What do I say when I read them aloud?
f_f0c42edbd803.answer: Say “freed people” or “Black Americans” instead. We read these sources as evidence of what people thought and did at the time, and we do not repeat slurs or period insults aloud. You can underline or point to the wording on the page when you discuss it. If a source is hard to read, you may step out for a moment without asking.

f_8a9a99db8621.question: If the Emancipation Proclamation already freed enslaved people in 1863, why did the country need the 13th Amendment?
f_8a9a99db8621.answer: The Emancipation Proclamation applied only to designated areas in rebellion, and some places, including Tennessee, were exempted. It was also a wartime order, so its force depended on the Union winning the war. The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, became part of the Constitution and ended slavery and involuntary servitude across the whole United States.

f_e0e6415b2602.question: Were the Black Codes just slavery under a new name?
f_e0e6415b2602.answer: Not exactly, and the difference matters when you write about them. The codes did not declare anyone enslaved. They used contracts, criminal penalties and hiring-out, and they applied to freed people and other Black residents because of their race. The codes did give freed people some rights, such as marrying and suing. They also limited where and how freed people could work, where they could go, and what land they could hold. Describe what each rule says and avoid calling it slavery unless the text does.

f_294b10816ec7.question: Why did Southern states get a vote on the 13th Amendment, and who wrote the Black Codes?
f_294b10816ec7.answer: Ratification needed three-fourths of the 36 states, which is 27. Under Johnson’s plan, the new Southern governments were required to ratify the amendment, and their votes counted. Those same governments, elected without a Black vote and left in white hands, wrote the Black Codes in the fall of 1865. Northern anger at the codes shaped what Congress did next.

f_1845ed4b2e47.question: Congress overrode Johnson’s veto. Was that the first time Congress had ever overridden a president?
f_1845ed4b2e47.answer: No. Congress had overridden vetoes before, on smaller matters. April 1866 was the first time it passed a major law over a presidential veto. An override needs a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate, so the vote showed how much Republican support there was in Congress.

f_23400a0bf0a8.question: What does “subject to its jurisdiction” mean in the 14th Amendment?
f_23400a0bf0a8.answer: It means a person is under the authority of the United States and its laws. The phrase limits who counts as a citizen by birth. The Civil Rights Act of 1866 had a similar limit: it left out “Indians not taxed.” At the time, Congress treated members of tribes as outside this group. Congress did not grant citizenship to Native Americans generally until the Indian Citizenship Act of 1924.

f_0ba96eda6955.question: Do the due process and equal protection clauses protect only citizens?
f_0ba96eda6955.answer: No. Both clauses use the word “person.” A state may not take the life, liberty or property of any person without due process of law. It may not deny any person within its borders the equal protection of its laws. The privileges or immunities clause is different. It speaks of “citizens of the United States.” Read the exact wording in Section 1 and notice whether it says “citizen” or “person.”

f_6588ffa1f628.question: Did army generals take over and run the Southern states?
f_6588ffa1f628.answer: Not completely. Civil governments kept operating, but under military authority. Each district’s general supervised voter registration and elections, and could use military courts and remove civil officials. Johnson vetoed the Act and called military rule in peacetime unconstitutional. Congress overrode his veto on March 2, 1867.

f_0138686f0f8d.question: If the 14th Amendment was already ratified or on its way, why did Congress need a 15th Amendment to protect Black men’s votes?
f_0138686f0f8d.answer: The 14th Amendment did not give anyone the vote. Its Section 2 only threatened to reduce a state’s representation if it denied the vote to adult male citizens, and it put the word male into the Constitution. Many Northern states still barred Black men from voting. The 15th Amendment, ratified February 3, 1870, set a national rule on race and voting.

f_20bbf4730980.question: Who was Hiram Revels, and why do historians still talk about him?
f_20bbf4730980.answer: Revels was born free in North Carolina and became a minister. Mississippi’s legislature chose him for the Senate. Democrats objected, but the Senate seated him on February 25, 1870, in a seat once held by Albert G. Brown. He was the first Black U.S. senator. Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi followed him in 1875.

f_84bc4bae05e4.question: The sources use words we are not allowed to say aloud. Why do we read them at all?
f_84bc4bae05e4.answer: We read them as evidence. They show what people did and how they spoke, and a historian needs that to understand the period. We read silently and use our own words when we discuss them, because saying the slurs aloud adds nothing to the analysis and can hurt people in the room. Anyone may step out for a moment without asking.

f_602f13ae97fb.question: What is habeas corpus, and why did it matter that the Ku Klux Klan Act let the president suspend it?
f_602f13ae97fb.answer: Habeas corpus is the right of a person who is being held to have a court review whether the government has a lawful reason to hold them. Suspending it meant officials could arrest and hold suspects without that review. This helped in places where Klan members had local protection. In October 1871 President Grant suspended it in nine South Carolina counties, and many arrests followed.

f_f1f32aed5c79.question: Why did Congress pass laws that used federal courts when states already had their own courts?
f_f1f32aed5c79.answer: In many Southern states, sheriffs, judges and juries would not act against the Klan. Some sympathized with it and some were afraid of it. State governments could not or would not protect Black voters and Republican officials. Congress relied on its power to enforce the 14th and 15th Amendments, so it made attacks on voting and equal rights federal crimes that federal courts could hear.
